source: Agreed with the repo owner, 2026-09-04. The Dungeons & Dividends rulebook (§13 item 3) explicitly leaves sub-stat scoring unspecified: 'Exact sub-stat scoring formulas (real dollars/inputs -> 8-20 scores) — this is the one piece the Claude Code build prompt still needs.' These are that missing piece.
confidenceNote: Calibration target: a US-population-median household scores 10 on every computed sub-stat, per the rulebook's own reading of 10-11 as 'neutral / average'. Median anchors are set from widely-published public figures (Census/BLS median earnings, BEA personal saving rate, SCF transaction-account balances) but are ROUNDED CONVENTIONS, not fitted distributions. Every other rung is an agreed shape, not a measurement. Edit this file to recalibrate; the engine reads it and holds no thresholds of its own.
note: Ladders interpolate linearly between rungs and clamp to 8-20. A sub-stat whose input was never entered is INCOMPLETE, never 8 and never 0 — see CLAUDE.md 'Empty != zero'.

methods.name: Feats of Strength
methods.blurb: Eighteen quick questions about what you'd actually do. No maths, nothing to revise, and no answer that makes you look daft — the honest one always scores.

methods.name: Point Buy
methods.blurb: Spend a pool of 45 points across the nine, however you like. Going high costs more each step, exactly as it does in 5e, so a 20 has to be paid for somewhere.

methods.name: Standard Array
methods.blurb: Nine fixed numbers, and you decide who gets what. The quickest honest route when you don't fancy answering questions tonight.

methods.name: Roll
methods.blurb: 4d6, drop the lowest, nine times. You get what you get — and like at a table, rolling can't reach 19 or 20.

methods.name: Homebrew
methods.blurb: Type the nine numbers yourself. Nothing is checked. For when you already know your character, or you just want to poke at it.

pointBuy.note: 8-15 costs are 5e's own table. 16-20 continue the same accelerating curve, since this system allows scores above 15 where 5e point buy does not. A 45-point pool buys all nine at 13, or a sharply peaked spread.

standardArray.note: Nine values averaging 11.3 — deliberately just above the population-median 10, since anyone building a sheet is already more engaged than average.

incomePower.medianAnchor: US median personal earnings for full-time year-round workers, ~$62k. Rounded to $60k = 10.

incomeTrajectory.medianAnchor: Median US nominal wage growth has run near 4%/yr recently and ~3%/yr long-run. 3% = 10, i.e. keeping pace is average.

hustleCapacity.unit: side income as a share of primary income
hustleCapacity.medianAnchor: Roughly a third of US adults report some side income, mostly small. Zero side income with no deployable skill = 8; zero but with a named, ready skill = 10.

readinessBonus.note: Added to the ladder result, then clamped. 'Ready' means a marketable skill named AND a stated willingness to deploy it inside a month.

liquidityAgility.unit: share of total assets reachable in a week without penalty
liquidityAgility.medianAnchor: Median US household holds very little outside home equity and retirement accounts; a ~10% penalty-free-liquid share is typical. 0.10 = 10.

structuralMobility.medianAnchor: Base 8 plus up to 12 checklist points. A median owner with modest equity, on-site work and a location tie lands near 10.

options.label: I rent
I own with 20%+ equity
I own with less than 20% equity
I owe more than the place is worth

checklist.question: Where your income can be earned from

options.label: Fully remote — location is irrelevant to my pay
Hybrid — I could stretch the radius
Must be on-site
Yes, and I have before
Yes, if the case were strong
Reluctantly
No

checklist.question: What ties you to where you live

options.label: Nothing that couldn't move with me
Soft ties — community, preference
School year, custody, or care obligations
A tie I would not break at any price

obligationFlex.unit: fixed costs as a share of total spending
obligationFlex.medianAnchor: Housing, insurance and required debt service run roughly 60-65% of spending for a typical US household. 0.65 = 10. LOWER is better, so this ladder descends.

savingsRate.medianAnchor: The US personal saving rate has run roughly 4-5% of disposable income. 6% of gross = 10.

consistency.unit: years sustaining the current savings rate
consistency.medianAnchor: One full year at a rate = 10. The rulebook defines this sub-stat as a track record 'through disruption, not just in a good year', so an untested record is capped.
consistency.untestedNote: Without a disruption survived (job loss, medical event, income drop of 20%+) the score is capped at 15 no matter the years, because the rulebook measures this THROUGH disruption.

reserveDepth.medianAnchor: Median US household transaction-account balance covers on the order of 1-1.5 months of spending. 1 month = 10. Rungs above that follow data/liquidity_benchmarks.json bands (3 = the usual floor, 6 = the usual full fund, 12 = deep).

negotiation.q: A job offer lands. The number is fine. Not great — fine. What actually happens next?

options.label: I counter. I've already looked up what this role pays elsewhere.
I counter, with a number I mostly made up on the spot.
I ask if there's any wiggle room and take whatever comes back.
I accept. Asking feels like pushing my luck.

negotiation.q: In the last three years, have you asked anyone for more money — a raise, a rate, a refund, a fee waived?

options.label: More than once, and it worked at least one of those times.
Once.
I asked, got a no, and haven't tried since.
Not once.

threatDetection.q: Someone you like and trust says they can get you a guaranteed 12% a year, no risk. Gut reaction?

options.label: “Guaranteed” and “no risk” at that number is the tell. I'm out.
I'd want it in writing, and I'd probably still pass.
I'd put a small amount in just to see.
Honestly? I'd be interested.

threatDetection.q: The last person who recommended you a financial product — do you know how they got paid for it?

options.label: Yes. I ask, because it changes what someone recommends.
I worked it out eventually.
No — it genuinely hadn't occurred to me.
Nobody's ever recommended me one.

network.q: You need paid work inside a month. Who can you actually call?

options.label: More than ten people who could plausibly connect me to something.
A handful — four or five names come to mind straight away.
One or two.
I'd be starting from job boards.

network.q: Think about your last few good things — work, a flat, a deal. How did they reach you?

options.label: Through people I know, more than once.
One of them came through someone I know.
All through public applications — but I could ask around if I had to.
All public applications, and asking around isn't really my thing.

selfAwareness.q: There's a specific situation that reliably makes you spend money you didn't plan to. Can you name it right now?

options.label: Yes — and I've actually built something in to stop it.
Yes, instantly. I just haven't done anything about it.
Sort of. It's more a mood than a moment.
No — it feels random from the inside.

selfAwareness.q: Last time you spent more than you meant to, what happened afterwards?

options.label: I worked out why and changed something about the setup.
I clocked the pattern and moved on.
I felt rubbish about it for a bit.
I try not to look at it too closely.

scenarioForesight.q: Your income stops tomorrow. How precisely do you know what happens next?

options.label: Precisely. It's written down, with dates and numbers.
I've thought it through properly — just never wrote it down.
Roughly. I know it would be bad.
I genuinely don't know, and I'd rather not find out.

scenarioForesight.q: Before your last purchase bigger than a month's rent, what did you actually compare?

options.label: Two real alternatives, and the option of not buying at all.
A couple of options — though I'd basically already decided.
Only whether I could afford it.
Nothing. I wanted it.

marketLiteracy.q: The market falls 30% over six weeks. Your money is in it. What do you actually do?

options.label: Nothing — or buy more. I decided this in advance, on a calm day.
Nothing, but I check the app far more than is good for me.
Move some to cash until it settles down.
Sell. I can always get back in later.

marketLiteracy.q: A friend says they're waiting for things to calm down before they start investing. You think:

options.label: Waiting has a cost too — that's time out of the market.
Fair enough, but they should pick a date to start regardless.
Sensible. Why buy into a mess.
I'd have no idea what to tell them.

personability.q: The people you share money with — partner, family, whoever. Where are they?

options.label: We set the plan together and we both actually follow it.
Supportive, but it's basically my job.
We avoid the topic.
We're pulling in opposite directions.
I don't share money with anyone.

personability.q: Last time you wanted someone in your household to change something about money, how did it go?

options.label: I made the case, they came round, and it stuck.
It worked for a while.
It turned into a row and nothing changed.
I didn't bring it up.
Doesn't apply to me.

instrumentLiteracy.q: Two funds hold basically the same companies. What do you look at first?

options.label: The ongoing fee — on identical holdings it's the bit I control.
How each one did over the last five years.
Whichever one my provider puts in front of me.
I wouldn't know where to start comparing them.

instrumentLiteracy.q: You're offered life cover that “builds a cash value you can borrow against”. Your response?

options.label: I'd compare it against plain term cover, and ask who gets paid for selling it.
I'd get someone I trust to look at it with me.
Sounds good — insurance and savings in one.
If the person seemed to know their stuff, I'd probably say yes.

taxLiteracy.q: A raise pushes you into a higher tax bracket. What happens to your take-home pay?

options.label: It goes up — only the money above the line is taxed at the higher rate.
It goes up, but I'd want to check by how much.
It could actually go down — that's the worry.
I've never really understood how brackets work.

taxLiteracy.q: Money going into a workplace pension or 401(k) before tax — what's the actual benefit?

options.label: I don't pay income tax on it this year; it's taxed when I take it out.
It grows without being taxed along the way.
There's a benefit, but I couldn't tell you what it is.
No idea — I just left whatever the default was.

quizNote: Two questions per declared sub-stat, each worth 0-6 points, summed onto a base of 8 — which lands exactly on the 8-20 scale with no rescaling. Every question is BEHAVIOURAL: it asks what you did or would do, not whether you can recall a definition. There is no arithmetic and nothing to revise for, because a quiz that makes someone feel stupid is a quiz they close. The zero-point option is always a real thing real people do, phrased so that picking it costs no dignity. `order` drives display sequence: the two questions for a sub-stat sit far apart, and the driest topics (tax, instruments) come last, once someone is already invested in the run.

hp.note: 1 HP = one week of expenses covered by liquid assets. Agreed with the owner 2026-09-04 to resolve the two incompatible HP definitions in rulebook §3A. See DECISIONS.md D-046.

classAssignment.note: The rulebook names seven levers (§4) but gives no assignment rule. Agreed approach: rank levers by the dollars actually moving through each, break ties on the class's two primary stats. The Keeper is scored on spending restraint rather than a pool, since expense reduction owns no asset.

levers.measure: Employment income (gross annual income less side income)
Spending restraint — how far below a same-income benchmark the household actually spends

classAssignment.keeperNote: The Keeper's 'pool' is the annual dollars NOT spent relative to a benchmark of 75% of gross income going out the door. Someone earning $100k and spending $50k is credited $25k of Keeper activity. This makes an aggressively frugal household able to out-rank a mid-sized portfolio, which is the whole point of the lever.

tier1Affinity.note: NOT rulebook content. The rulebook assigns a class from where money actually moves (§4), which a quiz-only sheet has none of. Ranking on the six main stats does not work either: with only INT, WIS and CHA scored, The Speculator (INT/WIS) is the only class with both primaries available and wins almost every time, while The Landholder (DEX/CON) can never appear at all. So a quiz-only LEANING ranks each class over three of the nine declared sub-stats it has real affinity with. It is explicitly a leaning, shown as such, and is replaced the moment dollars exist.

initiative.note: BRIEF §9.1: initiative = DEX modifier + an automation bonus. The reasoning is that initiative is how fast you act before you have decided to act, and money that moves itself acts without you. The bonus is NOT derived from a savings figure — it is a separate answer, because a large savings rate you execute by hand every month is exactly the case this is meant to distinguish. Unanswered means no bonus is shown at all, not +0.
